Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-boost-prompt-long-0140", "row_sha256": "555698fec6b9867aa30ba0616f5d5287f6d7945d26a83f4bbb17c323f5ca7d2e", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you help me turn these notes into a prompt for a useful numbered checklist for our household parcel pickup on Friday? i don't need you to make the checklist itself here, just shape the request so another assistant knows what to do. the pickup is booked for the 1–5 p.m. window at 18 Pine Row, apartment 2B. it is a walk-up building, not a house with a porch, and the front entry locks. the booking confirmation lists three parcels, and there are three ready to go: two cartons and one padded mailer. i want the eventual checklist to cover getting them ready, handling the pickup window, and what to do if the driver cannot complete the pickup, but it shouldn't pretend we know what the carrier will do in every situation.

for the parcel details: the first carton is a returned kettle going to Northstar Outfitters. it measures 16 by 12 by 8 inches and weighs 8 pounds. its prepaid label was printed Monday at the local library, the barcode is visible, the flap is taped, and the old shipping label has been removed. the second carton is a shoe return to the same retailer. it's 12 by 9 by 5 inches and weighs 3 pounds. that prepaid label is printed too and attached to the top. the small padded mailer is also a prepaid return, this one to a different shop; it is sealed and the label is attached on its broad side. i think all three labels look readable, but i haven't checked whether the pickup service has any package-specific restrictions, so don't claim that it accepts every shape just because the booking says three parcels. the confirmation does say three parcels, though.

there are a few home and access things that make the timing important. the callbox directory has the right name, M. Chen, for apartment 2B, but that buzzer sometimes fails to ring upstairs. the driver's entry isn't guaranteed. my cell number is on the booking and ends in 6142; the checklist can remind me to keep the phone nearby during the window, not repeat the full number or assume the driver will call. the hallway landing outside our apartment is narrow and shared, and we can't leave the parcels there because it is part of the exit route. there isn't a secure porch or another private outdoor spot for them. the building has a notice asking residents not to prop the front door open, so that can't be treated as an access plan either.

our timing isn't continuous. i'll be home until about 2:15 p.m. on Friday, then nobody from our apartment is expected back until my roommate Daniel gets home after 4 p.m. the booked window still runs until 5. Elena Ruiz, the building manager, is usually at the front desk on weekdays until 3:30 p.m., but i don't know whether she'll be there this Friday or whether she is allowed to take these parcels for us. she told me, “I can take a delivery if I'm at the desk, but please ask before leaving anything.” that was about deliveries in general, not a confirmation that she can accept this pickup. keep that distinction.

please arrange the request so the eventual assistant uses the information we actually have, and separates it from things that still need checking. i'd like the output to be a numbered checklist rather than a long explanation. it should first state the evidence or confirmed details from these notes, then give any recommendations that are supported by that evidence. where the carrier's process or the building's arrangements are unknown, make those points questions to verify instead of filling in an answer. don't turn my guess about readable labels into a verified inspection, and don't treat a booked three-parcel pickup as proof that the carrier has approved every package detail.

1. the checklist should have practical steps before Friday, during the 1–5 p.m. window, and for a missed or unsuccessful pickup. don't make up a new pickup time or say the driver will definitely arrive.
2. include the specific access issue with the intermittent buzzer, the locked entrance, the phone being nearby, and the restriction against leaving parcels in the shared hall or propping the door. keep the possible front-desk handoff conditional: only consider it if Elena confirms she is there and able to accept the parcels, and if the carrier's rules allow that arrangement. i haven't confirmed either point.
3. account for the fact that i'm home until roughly 2:15 and Daniel is expected after 4, leaving a gap when neither of us is expected home. if Elena confirms before Friday that the desk can accept them before she leaves at 3:30, that could matter for the gap; if she doesn't confirm, the checklist must not suggest leaving the parcels with her or in the hall anyway. don't claim she will be at the desk just because she usually is on weekdays.

please keep the three parcel descriptions straight, including which retailer each return goes to, their sizes and weights where i gave them, and the label and sealing details. do not add a fourth item or change the booked count. the request is for a checklist that helps us prepare and identify what to verify, not a guarantee of pickup, a carrier policy explanation presented as fact, or a message to the building manager. put open questions close to the checklist step they affect if that works, and keep the final output complete. one last thing: if the assistant can't establish from these notes whether the driver may call, whether the manager can receive a parcel, or whether the padded mailer is acceptable, it should leave each as an unresolved question rather than smoothing over the uncertainty. the pickup is still the Friday booking; don't silently convert it into a rescheduled collection.", "output": "Create a numbered checklist for preparing for and handling the household parcel pickup booked for Friday, 1–5 p.m., at 18 Pine Row, apartment 2B. Cover preparation before Friday, the pickup window, and what to do if the pickup is missed or cannot be completed. Do not guarantee that the driver will arrive or invent a different pickup time.

Start by separating the confirmed details in the notes from recommendations supported by those details. Keep carrier procedures and building arrangements that have not been confirmed as questions to verify, placed near the checklist steps they affect. Do not present assumptions as facts or explain unknown carrier policy as if it were established.

The booking confirmation lists three parcels, and three are ready: two cartons and one padded mailer. Preserve these descriptions:
- A returned kettle going to Northstar Outfitters, in a 16-by-12-by-8-inch carton weighing 8 pounds. Its prepaid label was printed Monday at the local library; the barcode is visible, the flap is taped, and the old shipping label has been removed.
- A shoe return going to Northstar Outfitters, in a 12-by-9-by-5-inch carton weighing 3 pounds. Its prepaid label is printed and attached to the top.
- A prepaid return to a different shop, in a small padded mailer. It is sealed, and its label is attached on the broad side.

The household believes all three labels look readable, but they have not verified that. Treat label readability as something to check, not a confirmed inspection. The booking lists three parcels, but that does not prove the carrier has approved every package detail or accepts every shape. In particular, whether the carrier permits the padded mailer is unknown. Do not add a parcel or change the booked count.

Account for the access arrangements: this is a walk-up building with a locked front entry, not a house with a porch. The callbox directory lists the correct name, M. Chen, for apartment 2B, but the buzzer sometimes fails to ring upstairs, so driver access is not guaranteed. The cell number on the booking ends in 6142; include a reminder to keep the phone nearby during the pickup window, but do not repeat the full number or assume the driver will call. The narrow shared hallway landing outside the apartment is part of the exit route, so parcels cannot be left there. There is no secure porch or other private outdoor location, and a building notice says not to prop the front door open. Do not suggest leaving parcels in the hallway or propping open the entrance.

Reflect the household’s Friday schedule accurately: one resident will be home until about 2:15 p.m.; nobody from the apartment is expected back until roommate Daniel arrives after 4 p.m. The pickup window continues until 5 p.m., leaving a gap when neither resident is expected to be home. Building manager Elena Ruiz is usually at the front desk on weekdays until 3:30 p.m., but her presence this Friday and her ability to accept these pickup parcels are unconfirmed. She said, “I can take a delivery if I'm at the desk, but please ask before leaving anything.” That statement concerned deliveries in general, not confirmation that she can accept this pickup.

A front-desk handoff may be considered only if Elena confirms she will be there and is able to accept the parcels, and the carrier’s rules allow the arrangement. Neither point has been confirmed. If Elena confirms before Friday that the desk can accept the parcels before she leaves at 3:30, note that this could matter during the household’s absence. If she does not confirm, do not suggest leaving parcels with her or in the hallway. Do not assume she will be at the desk simply because she usually works weekdays.

Make the checklist practical while keeping these uncertainties visible. Identify what needs checking about the carrier’s package requirements, the manager’s availability and permission, and whether the driver may call. If the notes do not establish an answer, leave it as an unresolved question rather than supplying one. The requested output is a complete numbered checklist to help prepare and identify what to verify—not a guarantee of pickup, an unsupported statement of carrier policy, or a message to the building manager. Keep the Friday booking unchanged."}]
